section.title: David Spares Saul Again
section.sectionRationale: For a second time the Ziphites betray David's location, and for a second time Saul comes hunting him with three thousand men, and for a second time David finds Saul utterly defenseless, this time asleep in the middle of his own camp. David slips in, takes the spear and water jug from beside Saul's head as proof, and again refuses to let Abishai strike the LORD's anointed. It is one movement: the settled conviction, tested twice now, that David must not seize the throne by violence but leave Saul's fate entirely to the LORD.
section.thesis: Given a second total opportunity to end his exile by killing Saul, David again refuses to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed, entrusting the timing and manner of Saul's downfall to God alone, a fixed resolve that marks him as a type of the greater King who would not grasp His kingdom by force.
section.frameNote: Five beats: Saul renews the hunt, verses 1 to 5; David and Abishai in the sleeping camp, verses 6 to 12; David's taunt across the ravine to Abner, verses 13 to 16; the exchange between David and Saul, verses 17 to 20; and Saul's confession and blessing, verses 21 to 25.

verses.text: Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is not David hiding on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon?”
So Saul, accompanied by three thousand chosen men of Israel, went down to the Wilderness of Ziph to search for David there.
Saul camped beside the road at the hill of Hachilah opposite Jeshimon, but David was living in the wilderness. When he realized that Saul had followed him there,
David sent out spies to verify that Saul had arrived.

Then David set out and went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw the place where Saul and Abner son of Ner, the general of his army, had lain down. Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him.
David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?” “I will go with you,” answered Abishai.

That night David and Abishai came to the troops, and Saul was lying there asleep in the inner circle of the camp, with his spear stuck in the ground by his head. And Abner and the troops were lying around him.

Abishai said to David, “Today God has delivered your enemy into your hand. Now, therefore, please let me thrust the spear through him into the ground with one stroke. I will not need to strike him twice!”
But David said to Abishai, “Do not destroy him, for who can extend a {{yad|hand}} against the LORD’s {{mashiach|anointed}} and be guiltless?”
David added, “As surely as the LORD lives, the LORD Himself will strike him down; either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish.
But the LORD forbid that I should extend my hand against the LORD’s anointed. Instead, take the spear and water jug by his head, and let us go.”

So David took the spear and water jug by Saul’s head, and they departed. No one saw them or knew about it, nor did anyone wake up; they all remained asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them.
Then David crossed to the other side and stood atop the mountain at a distance; there was a wide gulf between them.
And David shouted to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, “Will you not answer me, Abner?” “Who are you who calls to the king?” Abner replied.
So David said to Abner, “You are a man, aren’t you? And who in Israel is your equal? Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him?

This thing you have done is not good. As surely as the LORD lives, all of you deserve to die, since you did not protect your lord, the LORD’s anointed. Now look around. Where are the king’s spear and water jug that were by his head?”

units.label: David appeals to Saul
units.note: what evil is in my hand

verses.text: Then Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, “Is that your voice, David my son?” “It is my voice, my lord and king,” David said.
And he continued, “Why is my lord pursuing his servant? What have I done? What evil is in my hand?

Now please, may my lord the king hear the words of his servant: If the LORD has stirred you up against me, then may He accept an offering. But if men have done it, may they be cursed in the presence of the LORD! For today they have driven me away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’
So do not let my blood fall to the ground far from the presence of the LORD. For the king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains.”
Then Saul replied, “I have sinned. Come back, David my son. I will never harm you again, because today you considered my life precious. I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!”
“Here is the king’s spear,” David answered. “Let one of the young men come over and get it.

May the LORD repay every man for his {{tsedaqah|righteousness}} and faithfulness. For the LORD delivered you into my hand today, but I would not extend my hand against the LORD’s {{mashiach|anointed}}.
As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and rescue me from all trouble.”
Saul said to him, “May you be blessed, David my son. You will accomplish great things and will surely prevail.” So David went on his way, and Saul returned home.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one. Saul was set apart for the throne by Samuel's anointing oil, and even though he hunts David without cause, David twice refuses to lift a hand against him for this reason alone, verses 9 and 23. The office belongs to the LORD's own choosing, not to whoever can seize it by the sword.

tsedaqah.gloss: Righteousness, right conduct, covenant faithfulness. David asks that the LORD Himself repay every man his tsedaqah, resting his reward on God's just character rather than on Saul's unstable gratitude, since Saul's own promises have already failed once before, in chapter 24.

yad.gloss: Hand, the seat of a person's power or action. Twice David refuses to extend his yad against the LORD's anointed, and he later asks Saul what evil is in his own hand, verse 18, framing the whole episode as a question of whose hand will act, and whose hand will be found innocent.

basic.context: This is the second time in as many episodes that David has Saul completely in his power. The Ziphites betray his location again, Saul comes hunting him with three thousand men, and David slips by night into the very heart of the sleeping camp, right beside Saul's head. His companion Abishai begs to end it with one thrust of the spear. But David refuses, a second time, to kill the man God anointed as king. Instead he takes the spear and water jug as evidence and shouts the proof across the valley at dawn, rebuking Abner for failing to guard the king. Confronted, Saul again confesses his sin and blesses David, though the two do not travel home together; David still will not trust his safety to Saul's word. The whole scene asks how an anointed but rejected king is meant to wait for God's kingdom rather than seize it for himself.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing David's own conviction about a specific king whom God had anointed; it is not a general command that every wrong must go unanswered or that lawful justice may never be pursued. What it does teach every reader is a settled trust that vindication and timing belong to the LORD, especially when we are wronged by those set in authority over us.
basic.originalLanguages: David will not raise a yad, hand, against the LORD's mashiach, anointed, even though Saul hunts him without cause. At the end he asks the LORD to repay every man his tsedaqah, righteousness, the very thing Saul's own word cannot reliably deliver.
basic.typology: David, God's anointed yet still uncrowned king, refuses again and again to seize the throne by violence, choosing instead to wait for God to act in His own time and way. This looks forward to great David's greater Son, who though truly King would not call down legions of angels or grasp an earthly throne by force, entrusting Himself instead to the Father's justice and timing.
basic.christ: David's refusal to strike the LORD's anointed, even when a companion urges it and the opportunity is total, anticipates the pattern fulfilled perfectly in Jesus Christ. Jesus, the true Anointed One, refused Peter's sword in Gethsemane and would not summon armies of angels to seize His kingdom by force, choosing instead the Father's path through suffering to glory. Like David, He entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, and received His kingdom not by grasping but by humble obedience even to death, only then exalted by God Himself.
basic.god: God is shown as the true King over kings, the one who alone has the right to remove Saul in His own timing, whether by natural death or in battle. He casts a supernatural deep sleep over Saul's whole camp so David can act without bloodshed, and it is to Him that David appeals for vindication and reward rather than to human strength or opportunity. Even Saul, in a fleeting moment of honesty, recognizes that David's restraint flows from valuing what belongs to the LORD.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 24 records the first time David spares Saul, in the cave at En-gedi. 1 Peter 2 says Christ entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. Matthew 26 shows Jesus refusing the sword in Gethsemane. Romans 12 says vengeance belongs to the LORD. Philippians 2 says Christ did not grasp at equality with God but humbled Himself.
basic.oneStory: David's second refusal to kill Saul is one more step in the long story of a king who will not seize his throne by violence, trusting the LORD's timing instead. It anticipates the true Anointed One, Jesus, who also refused to grasp His kingdom by force, and whose patient trust in the Father's justice becomes the pattern for all who suffer unjustly while awaiting God's vindication.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a deliberate double of chapter 24, and the doubling is itself the argument. Both episodes share the same skeleton, a Ziphite betrayal, a total opportunity, a companion urging violence, David's refusal on the ground that Saul is the LORD's anointed, a piece of physical evidence taken rather than a life taken, a shouted exchange across a distance at daybreak, and Saul's confession. Repeating the pattern so closely tells the reader this was never a single burst of restraint that happened to hold; it is David's fixed policy, tested twice under the most extreme provocation available and proven both times.

The scene inside the camp, verses 6 to 12, is built for suspense through sheer physical detail, the inner circle, the spear stuck in the ground by Saul's head, Abner and the troops lying around him, and then the single explanatory clause that removes any danger for David before it can be felt, a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them, verse 12. The narrator lets the reader feel the risk and then reveals it was never real risk at all, only staged suspense, since the whole scene was safe from its first step.

David's shouted speech to Abner, verses 14 to 16, functions as public theater rather than private conversation, meant to be overheard by the whole camp and by Saul himself, and it escalates in three moves, a taunt about Abner's failed duty, a legal charge, all of you deserve to die, and finally the unanswerable proof, the missing spear and jug. Only after this public vindication does David turn to address Saul directly, verses 17 to 20, in markedly gentler, more personal language, my lord and king, a shift in register that marks the difference between defending his innocence before witnesses and appealing, man to man, to the king who still holds his life in balance.
context.historical:
The wilderness of Ziph lay in the rugged hill country south of Hebron, broken terrain of ravines and scrub that had already sheltered David once before, 1 Samuel 23:14 to 24, and the Ziphites' second betrayal, verse 1, shows how little safety even friendly territory offered a fugitive with a price on his head and a king determined to keep hunting him. A royal campaign of this size, three thousand chosen men, verse 2, would have posted watches and kept its commanding general close to the king for exactly this reason, to prevent the kind of infiltration that in fact occurs; that Abner, described elsewhere as a seasoned and capable commander, 2 Samuel 2:8 to 9, could be caught so completely unaware makes the narrator's explanation, a deep sleep from the LORD, verse 12, the only plausible account of what happened.

The items David takes, the spear and the water jug kept by a sleeping king's head, verse 7, were not incidental camp gear but recognizable marks of the king's own presence, easily identified at a distance the next morning and impossible for Abner to explain away. Ancient Near Eastern kings commonly kept a weapon within reach even at rest, and Saul's spear in particular has already functioned earlier in the book as an extension of his own hand, the very weapon he hurled at David in the palace, 1 Samuel 18:11 and 19:10, so that David now holds, without using it, the same spear that had once been thrown to kill him.
context.canonical:
This is the second and final test of the principle chapter 24 first establishes, and by repeating it Samuel's book closes off any reading of the earlier episode as an isolated moment of emotion rather than settled conviction; between the two lies chapter 25, where the same restraint is tested yet again, this time not against God's anointed but against a private insult, showing the same discipline of leaving vengeance to the LORD applied consistently across every kind of provocation David faces in this stretch of his story.

The scene's central conviction, that no one may lift a hand against the LORD's anointed and remain innocent, verse 9, becomes a settled category the rest of the Old Testament assumes rather than argues for; even David's own later grief over Saul's death, 2 Samuel 1:14 to 16, treats striking down the LORD's anointed as an offense deserving death regardless of who commits it or under what provocation. The pattern also anticipates how the New Testament will treat civil authority more broadly, submission and patience toward flawed or hostile rulers rather than private violence, Romans 13:1 to 7, 1 Peter 2:13 to 17, a posture this chapter models in miniature toward one particular, deeply flawed king.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
By narrating a near duplicate of chapter 24, the author means to remove any doubt that David's restraint was circumstantial, a mercy shown once under the emotional pressure of a cave and a cut robe. Here the provocation is, if anything, greater, Saul again hunts him with an army after having already confessed his guilt once, and Abishai's counsel to strike is more decisive and less easily refused than a robe quietly cut in the dark. That David refuses again, with the same reasoning and almost the same words, tells the first hearers that this is who David is, not merely what David once did.

The author also wants Israel to see how a legitimate claim to the throne is meant to be pursued, publicly, with evidence rather than violence, and before witnesses rather than in secret. David does not simply spare Saul and slip away; he stages his own vindication in the full hearing of Saul's army, forcing Abner and, through him, all Israel to reckon openly with what kind of man David is and what kind of king Saul has shown himself to be. The intended effect is to establish beyond dispute, before David ever takes the throne, that it was given to him rather than seized by him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes David's specific conviction toward a specific king whom God had anointed to office; it does not prescribe passive submission to every wrongdoer or forbid the lawful pursuit of justice through appointed means. David still sends spies, verse 4, still arms and moves his men, and still publicly exposes wrongdoing, verses 15 to 16, so his restraint is not the same thing as inaction or silence about wrong; he actively defends his innocence, he simply refuses to do it by killing the man in front of him. Reading this chapter as a blanket command never to resist or resent any wrong misses that David pursues real vindication, only by evidence and appeal rather than by the sword.

What does transfer as abiding instruction is the deeper principle beneath the specific case, that those under authority, even flawed or hostile authority, are not thereby licensed to remove that authority by violence whenever the opportunity presents itself, and that a person wronged can trust the LORD's own timing for vindication rather than forcing the issue by their own hand. Saul's shifting, unstable repentance in this chapter is a further caution: gratitude for restraint does not by itself prove lasting change, so the text also teaches a wise discernment about when trust is warranted and when only distance is.

debates.question: Why does David take the spear and water jug rather than simply withdrawing unseen?

views.label: Public proof of restraint
views.case: Taking these items let David prove beyond doubt, from a safe distance the next morning, that he had stood near enough to kill Saul and chose not to, closing off in advance any future accusation that he was secretly plotting rebellion.

views.label: Evidence that also indicted the guard
views.case: The missing royal spear and water jug proved not only David's restraint but Abner's catastrophic failure to protect the king, turning the same evidence into both a defense of David's innocence and a public humiliation of Saul's own commander, verses 15 to 16.

debates.bearing: Either way, David sought vindication through visible proof rather than through violence or through his own unsupported word, showing that being in the right before God does not require winning the argument by force.

debates.question: Does Saul's confession in verse 21 show genuine, if fragile, repentance, or only a repeated pattern of hollow remorse?

views.label: A real, if unstable, softening
views.case: Saul's words go further here than in chapter 24, adding an explicit blessing over David's future greatness, you will accomplish great things and will surely prevail, verse 25, which reads as more than a bare apology and suggests some genuine, if short lived, conviction.

views.label: A repeated but ultimately hollow pattern
views.case: Saul had said nearly identical words once before, chapter 24, and would return to hostility soon after; the almost verbatim repetition suggests an emotional response to being caught rather than a durable change, since Saul offers David no restored place, no protection, and no end to the pursuit that resumes by the next chapter's opening.

debates.bearing: David himself does not stake his safety on the answer either way; he returns to his own camp rather than to Saul's, a discernment that distinguishes a felt emotion of sorrow from a proven, sustained change of behavior.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's vocabulary keeps returning to one small word, hand, yad, and lets it carry nearly the whole moral argument. Abishai sees Saul's helplessness as God's gift into David's hand, verse 8, and reaches for his own hand to end it with one stroke; David answers that no one may extend a hand against the LORD's anointed and be innocent, verse 9, repeats the same refusal in verse 11, and later asks Saul directly what evil is in my hand, verse 18, turning the moral question back onto himself before Saul can accuse him of anything. The word appears again in verse 23, I would not extend my hand against the LORD's anointed, so that by the chapter's end the entire episode has been narrated as a contest not of armies but of whose hand would act, and whose hand would be found clean.

David's title for Saul, the LORD's anointed, mashiach, is the same word later Scripture reserves for the coming Messiah, and its force here is entirely about office rather than character, Saul's anointing, not his conduct, is what stays David's hand, since the office belongs to the LORD's own choice and not to whoever proves strong enough to seize it. David extends the same logic to himself in verse 10, refusing even to specify how or when Saul's end will come, either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish, a studied vagueness that hands the timing and the manner entirely to God rather than naming a preferred outcome.

The chapter's final word belongs to another root, tsedaqah, righteousness or right dealing, verse 23, which David asks the LORD to repay to every man according to his own conduct. Resting his hoped for reward on God's righteousness rather than on Saul's gratitude is a quiet but pointed choice of words, since Saul's own promises, however sincerely meant in the moment, have already failed once before in chapter 24 and prove no more durable here. The verb behind David's earlier statement that Saul deserved to die, all of you deserve to die, verse 16, carries the sense of a legal sentence rather than a private grievance, framing Abner's negligence as a matter for judgment, not merely embarrassment.

typology.type: David refusing a second total opportunity to seize the throne by violence, verses 8 to 11
typology.fulfillment: Christ, the true Anointed One, who would not grasp an earthly kingdom by force even when every advantage in the moment lay with Him, but received all authority from the Father through suffering and resurrection rather than conquest, Philippians 2:6 to 11. David's restraint is repeatable but still partial, tested twice under pressure; Christ's is total and without any moment of hesitation, since He never once reached for Peter's sword or called for angelic legions, Matthew 26:52 to 53.

typology.type: David entrusting his cause to the LORD rather than avenging himself, verses 10 and 23
typology.fulfillment: Christ, who when reviled did not revile in return, entrusting Himself instead to Him who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. David still hopes for a future reward for his own righteousness, verse 23, weighing his own conduct against Saul's; Christ, who alone is perfectly righteous, receives His reward not as payment owed for merely adequate behavior but as the Father's vindication of a finished, flawless obedience carried all the way to a cross, Philippians 2:9 to 11, a righteousness David could only imitate from a distance.

typology.type: A public, evidentiary vindication before hostile witnesses, verses 13 to 16
typology.fulfillment: David stages his innocence in full view of Saul's own army rather than defending himself quietly or in a private hearing, forcing a whole camp to reckon openly with the evidence in his hand. Christ's vindication comes even more publicly and finally, an empty tomb before multiple witnesses over forty days, Acts 1:3, and one day every eye seeing Him at His return, Revelation 1:7, a vindication that needs no missing spear as proof because death itself is the enemy that is visibly overturned.

study.christ:
David's second refusal to kill Saul, made under greater provocation than the first and with a companion actively urging the fatal stroke, anticipates a pattern that Scripture's greater King fulfills without any hesitation at all. Where David needed Abishai's urging to even test his own resolve, and needed a second whole episode to prove the first was no accident, the New Testament shows a Son of David who never once wavers toward the shortcut of force, even facing an arrest, a mock trial, and a cross far worse than anything Saul's army threatened.

David still calculates a future reward for his own righteousness, verse 23, measuring his conduct against Saul's and asking the LORD to repay each man in kind; the true King needed no such balancing, being already perfectly righteous, and instead of collecting a reward earned by good behavior He secured reward for others by giving up what was rightfully His, becoming poor so that many might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. His obedience was not merely restraint from one violent act but a whole life offered up, and a death accepted willingly rather than merely avoided.

The chapter's insistence that the manner and timing of an enemy's downfall belong entirely to God, either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish, verse 10, finds its deepest answer in how the Father dealt with the greatest enemy humanity faces. That final enemy was not defeated by military conquest at the first coming but by a death and a resurrection, with the visible, final defeat of every hostile power entrusted to a day still to come, 1 Corinthians 15:24 to 26. Like David waiting rather than striking, believers now live between a victory already accomplished in principle and a victory not yet finished in plain sight, trusting the same patient justice David trusted when he sheathed his sword a second time.

Even the small detail of David's restraint being tested twice rather than once has its own quiet echo in Christ's story, since His own resolve to walk the Father's path was tested more than once as well, first in a wilderness at the very start of His ministry and again in a garden on the very night He was betrayed, and each time the answer was the same steady obedience David could only manage in part.
study.god:
God is shown here as the true King over kings, the one who alone has the right to remove Saul in His own timing, whether by natural death or in battle, verse 10, a right David explicitly declines to claim for himself even though ending Saul's reign that very night lies entirely within his power. This is providence exercised through withheld action as much as through decisive intervention; God is as present in David's refusal to strike as He would be in any miracle, since it is God's own claim on Saul's life, not merely David's personal restraint, that keeps the spear from falling.

God's sovereignty over the physical world is displayed with almost comic understatement, a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them, verse 12, six words that quietly explain how two men walked past an entire army's watch, took the king's own weapon from beside his head, and walked out again undetected. The narrator offers no theophany, no angel, no voice, only a brief clause that credits the whole outcome to God's direct, unseen action over ordinary soldiers doing an ordinary job badly because God had made it so, a small but telling reminder that the LORD does not always need a spectacle to accomplish exactly what He intends.

God is also the standard by which David measures true reward, appealing not to Saul's fickle promises but to the LORD's own righteous character, may the LORD repay every man for his righteousness and faithfulness, verse 23, a request that assumes God sees, remembers, and eventually settles accounts that human relationships cannot be trusted to settle. And in a fleeting, honest moment even Saul is made to confess what David's restraint reveals about the God behind it, you considered my life precious, verse 21, a fragile acknowledgment that the LORD's anointed office, and the God who gave it, still commanded real weight even in the heart of a king bent on murder. That the same God who casts a whole camp into sleep also stoops to let a fallen king glimpse, however briefly, what he has forfeited shows a justice that never stops being patient even while it remains perfectly just.

crossReferences.note: The first time David spares Saul, cutting only the corner of his robe in a cave at En-gedi rather than harming him, establishing the same principle this chapter repeats under harsher provocation and confirms as settled conviction rather than a single act of mercy.

Saul had earlier hurled this very spear at David twice in his own house, so David now holds, without using it, the identical weapon that had once been thrown to kill him, a quiet reversal the narrator leaves the reader to notice.

David later has a man executed for merely claiming to have killed Saul, treating violence against the LORD's anointed as a capital offense regardless of Saul's own condition or consent, the same conviction voiced here carried through to its logical end.

Jesus refuses Peter's sword and the offer of twelve legions of angels, choosing the Father's path rather than seizing deliverance by force, the pattern of refusing an available violent shortcut that David models twice over against Saul.

Christ entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly rather than retaliating when reviled and suffering unjustly, the very posture David describes when he leaves Saul's fate to the LORD's own day or battle, verse 10.
Never take revenge, but leave room for God's wrath, the principle Abishai's counsel tempts David to abandon and that David instead holds to without any Abigail present to persuade him this time.

Christ did not grasp at equality with God but humbled Himself, and was afterward exalted by the Father, the pattern David's twice repeated restraint from seizing the throne by force anticipates in miniature.

Samuel's earlier sentence that the LORD has torn the kingdom from Saul and given it to a better neighbor is the settled fact David refuses to hasten by his own hand, content instead to let God's own timing bring it to pass.

Do not say, I will repay evil, wait for the LORD, and He will save you, a proverb that reads like a summary of exactly the discipline David practices here rather than any specific incident it describes.

study.oneStory:
The Old Testament keeps asking how God's chosen king will finally arrive, by the world's ordinary method of conquest and force, or by some other way entirely, and this chapter answers with unusual clarity for a story so early in David's rise. Twice now the throne has lain within reach of a single, undetected stroke, and twice David has set the sword down, choosing instead to let the LORD remove one king and install another in His own time. The repetition matters because it turns a single dramatic choice into an established character, this is not what David did once under pressure, it is who David has become.

That choice becomes a load bearing beam for everything the rest of Scripture builds upon it. Israel's later kings, for all their failures, inherit a throne understood to be God's gift rather than a prize for the strongest sword arm, and centuries later the true Son of David stands in the same position David once did, holding real power to seize a kingdom by force and refusing it, trusting instead the Father's timing through suffering to glory rather than through conquest, Philippians 2:6 to 11.

The episode also anticipates how the story eventually resolves every enemy who, like Saul, opposes God's anointed and yet is met with patience rather than instant destruction. God's people have always had to hold together two things that feel like they should pull apart, real, present evil that deserves judgment, and a God who delays that judgment for reasons of His own, sometimes for the sake of undeserved mercy, 2 Peter 3:9. David's willingness to leave Saul in God's hands rather than his own becomes a small, repeatable model for every believer who must wait for a wrong to be righted that they cannot and should not right themselves, until the day the true King returns to settle every account in full, Revelation 19:11 to 16.

quiz.q: When David found Saul asleep in the camp a second time, what did he do?

options.text: He refused to let Abishai kill Saul, insisting no one may harm the LORD's anointed, and instead took the spear and water jug as proof.
options.note: Verses 9-12 give David's explicit reasoning and his chosen action.

options.text: He took the spear and water jug from beside Saul's head and quietly left the camp.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits David's stated theological reason for sparing Saul.

options.text: He debated killing Saul and let Abishai make the final call.
options.note: The opposite is true; David commanded Abishai not to touch Saul, the decision was David's alone.

options.text: He killed Saul immediately with Abishai's spear.
options.note: David explicitly forbade this and refused to strike Saul at all.

quiz.q: Why does David refuse to kill Saul, in his own stated words?

options.text: Because Saul is the LORD's anointed, and it is God alone who must remove him, whether by death, battle, or His own timing.
options.note: Verses 9-11 give this as David's reason, twice repeated.

options.text: Because killing a reigning king would break Israelite law.
options.note: David never appeals to a legal statute; his stated reason is Saul's anointed office, not a point of law.

options.text: Because Abishai talked him out of striking.
options.note: The reverse is true; Abishai urged the killing and David refused him.

options.text: Because he feared Saul's army would retaliate if he was caught.
options.note: The text gives no such fear; David and Abishai left completely undetected.

quiz.q: What proof did David use to confront Abner about failing to protect Saul?

options.text: The king's spear and water jug, taken from right beside Saul's sleeping head.
options.note: Verse 16 has David point to these missing items as evidence Abner failed his duty.

options.text: A report from spies that Saul's guard had grown careless.
options.note: David did send spies earlier, verse 4, but the direct proof shown to Abner was the physical spear and jug.

options.text: David's own unsupported testimony, without any physical evidence.
options.note: David had visible, physical proof in hand, not merely his word.

options.text: The corner of Saul's robe cut off earlier.
options.note: That was the proof used in chapter 24, at En-gedi, not in this later episode.

quiz.q: How does Saul respond when he recognizes David's voice and sees the evidence?

options.text: He confesses that he has sinned and played the fool, and he blesses David, predicting he will prevail.
options.note: Verses 21 and 25 record Saul's confession and his blessing over David.

options.text: He apologizes but insists he has done nothing wrong.
options.note: Saul explicitly says, 'I have sinned,' which is more than a bare apology without admission.

options.text: He orders his men to seize David at once.
options.note: Saul does the opposite, calling David 'my son' and promising never to harm him again.

options.text: He denies that the voice calling to him is David's at all.
options.note: Saul immediately recognizes and names David's voice, verse 17.

quiz.q: What does David ask the LORD to do in verse 23?

options.text: To repay every man for his righteousness and faithfulness, since David would not harm the LORD's anointed though he had the chance.
options.note: Verse 23 records this exact request, resting David's reward on God's just character.

options.text: To grant David the throne immediately, that same day.
options.note: David does trust God for his future, but his stated request here is about righteous reward, not an immediate crowning.

options.text: To punish Saul at once for hunting him.
options.note: David explicitly leaves Saul's fate to God's timing in verse 10, not to instant punishment here.

options.text: To make Saul forget the whole episode had happened.
options.note: David wants the episode remembered as proof of his innocence, not forgotten.

quiz.q: How does David's restraint in this chapter point toward Christ?

options.text: Like David refusing to seize the throne by violence, Jesus refused to grasp His kingdom by force, trusting the Father's justice and timing instead.
options.note: Matthew 26:52-53 and Philippians 2:6-11 draw exactly this connection.

options.text: It shows only that violence is generally an unwise strategy.
options.note: There is a true principle here, but it understates the specific theological point about God's anointed and God's timing.

options.text: It has no real connection to Christ, being only political strategy on David's part.
options.note: Scripture itself draws this connection through the pattern of the anointed one and the theme of entrusting oneself to God's justice.

options.text: It shows David lacked the courage that Christ later displayed.
options.note: The text presents David's restraint as deliberate conviction and courage, not cowardice.

questions: David again had Saul's life in his hands but chose to leave vindication to God. Where are you tempted to 'help God along' by taking justice into your own hands rather than trusting His timing?
David calls Saul 'the LORD's anointed' even while fleeing his violence. How does honoring the office or position someone holds change the way you deal with people who wrong you?
Saul confesses his sin, yet the pattern of hostility repeats, and David still keeps his distance. How do you discern between someone's genuine sorrow and a proven change in behavior?
David asks the LORD, not Saul, to repay his righteousness. Where do you look for validation or reward instead of resting in God's approval?

Jesus refused to seize His kingdom by force, entrusting Himself to the Father's justice. What would it look like for you to release a difficult situation into God's hands this week rather than forcing an outcome?

translationNotes.note: The LORD's anointed renders mashiach, the same word later used of the Messiah; here it names Saul's God-given office rather than his personal character, which is why David honors it even while fleeing Saul's violence.

Either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish leaves the manner and timing of Saul's end entirely open, an intentional refusal by David to specify how or when, since that belongs to God alone.

If the LORD has stirred you up... may He accept an offering, but if men have done it, may they be cursed reflects an ancient assumption that unexplained royal hostility might have a hidden divine cause, while still holding any human instigators fully responsible for their part.
